rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (9 items)
rationale: A whole-country frame: every person in Sweden first diagnosed with nonaffective psychosis (ICD-10 F20-F29) aged 16-45 between 2006 and 2016, identified from the National Patient Register covering inpatient and specialized outpatient care. For a national first-episode psychosis population this is the strongest frame available.

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (9 items)
rationale: Total enumeration with no sampling step: all register-identified cases were included and linked by the personal identification number across four national registers.

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (9 items)
rationale: N = 21,551, far above any precision requirement for a prevalence.
source_location: Results, Sample Characteristics, p. 940; Table 1, p. 941

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (9 items)
rationale: Table 1 describes age and age band, sex, country of birth, specific first-diagnosis ICD-10 code, source of the first diagnosis, education level, prior antipsychotic use and baseline income from work; the Swedish sickness-absence and disability-pension systems are described in detail.

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (9 items)
rationale: Two coverage failures. First, 5,144 people already on disability pension at first diagnosis were excluded from the analysed cohort; disability pension is granted for permanently reduced work capacity, so the exclusion removes precisely those least likely to be employed and raises every employment percentage by an unknown amount. Second, the denominator behind the year-by-year percentages is never stated and cannot be the full 21,551 given accrual to 2016 against linkage ending 31 December 2016 and a median follow-up of 4.8 years.
source_location: Methods, Study Design and Statistical Analysis, p. 940; Figure 1 footnote, p. 942

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (9 items)
rationale: ICD-10 F20-F29 recorded in the National Patient Register by specialist inpatient or outpatient services, with the exact code distribution printed in Table 1. Diagnoses are clinical rather than research-interview based, and F29 (unspecified nonorganic psychosis) accounts for 43.0%, but the identification method is valid and uniform.

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (9 items)
rationale: The employment measure is applied uniformly from registers, which is reliable, but it is only partly specified: the paper states that the starting point was 'categorization by Statistics Sweden, where people were categorized as employed or not employed based on income' without giving that income rule, and then that 'people were assigned to the occupational activity generating income for more than 6 months yearly'. The classification therefore cannot be reproduced, and what it measures is a dominant main activity rather than any paid employment.

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (9 items)
rationale: The occupational-activity series is presented as a stacked figure of percentages with no counts, no denominators, no confidence intervals and no account of how censoring was handled. The paper's considerable statistical apparatus (stratified within-subject Cox models, PRE2DUP exposure modelling, nine sensitivity analyses) is directed entirely at the work-disability hazard ratios, not at these prevalences, which are reported only as context.

rob_tool_version: JBI critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies (9 items)
rationale: Register linkage removes non-response as such, and only education had missing data. But follow-up ends at 'death, emigration, DP, or the end of data linkage', and the number of people contributing to each yearly percentage is never reported, so the effective response rate at years 1 to 5 is unknown and the exclusion of prevalent disability pensioners is not managed or quantified anywhere.
